Mc Worter

GeometryTrianglesConstructions
Game: Two squares grow on two sides of a triangle; watch the point D and the triangle it makes with the squares' far corners.
How to play: Drag A, B or C, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press the buttons to show names, rotation lines and hint marks.
Look for the math

Build two squares that share the corner C of a triangle. Complete the parallelogram ADBC. Something unexpected happens at its fourth corner D: the two far corners of the squares and D make an isosceles right triangle, however you move C. The live cut-the-knot page has replaced its old Java applet with a GeoGebra picture; the archived page from 2010 still embeds CODE="McWorter" and states the claim below.

The two squares

On side CA the square has far corners B_a and B_c; on side CB it has A_b and A_c. The applet's FormSquare makes them with a quarter rotation: A_b = B + R(C − B) and B_a = A + R⁻¹(C − A), where R is a quarter turn and R⁻¹ the opposite one. The red segment joins A_b and B_a, and M is its midpoint.

Why M never moves

Write the points as complex numbers a, b, g and let i² = −1. Then A_b = b + (g − b)i, B_a = a − (g − a)i, and

M = (A_b + B_a)/2 = (a + b)/2 + (a − b)i/2.

Every g cancels: this is Bottema's theorem. The logic test checks this closed form against the applet's own rotate-and-average calculation on 2,730 triples of point positions and 600 random ones.

The parallelogram ADBC

The applet sets D = A + B − C, the fourth corner of the parallelogram with corners A, D, B, C. That means AD = CB and BD = CA. The hint marks the matching sides: AC = AB_a = BD and BC = BA_b = AD. So triangles AB_aD and BDA_b have all three sides equal in pairs — they are congruent, and in particular DA_b = DB_a. That is the isosceles part of McWorter's observation.

The right angle at D

Let u = A − C and v = B − C. The two legs at D are v − R(u) and u + R(v). A quarter turn is skew, so dot(v, R(u)) = −dot(u, R(v)): the dot product of the legs is zero and their lengths are equal. Hence ∠B_aDA_b = 90° — the exact claim on the article's page — and the test confirms it at every non-collapsed case in the grid and random samples. If the two far corners both land on D, the triangle shrinks to a point and there is no angle to speak of.

This is not the sibling applet McWorter2's claim. That one replaces the squares with similar parallelograms (K = (slider + 20)/20, angle from a second slider) and still finds M independent of C; it makes no right-angle claim at D, and the right angle at D generally fails for slanted parallelograms.

Try dragging C onto the line AB, then far away on the other side. Turn on the hint to watch the matching ticks and the square corner at D survive every move.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
